cls: Fat-soluble vitamin - supplement for vitamin A deficiency
pharm: An essential fat-soluble vitamin and its retinoid metabolites are required for rhodopsin formation and night vision, normal differentiation and integrity of epithelial tissues, immune function, growth, and reproduction; supplementation corrects or prevents deficiency.
quick: Deficiency: 10,000-50,000 IU/day orally per severity; RDA ~3,000 IU (900 mcg RAE) men, 2,310 IU (700 mcg) women
Take with food (a meal containing fat) to aid absorption
Do NOT exceed ~10,000 IU/day - high doses are teratogenic; routine prenatal amounts are safe
Recommended intakes are safe; avoid high-dose supplementation
Caution - vitamin A can accumulate in chronic kidney disease (risk of toxicity)
Avoid high doses; chronic excess and pre-existing liver disease cause hepatotoxicity
Avoid heavy alcohol - additive hepatotoxicity with vitamin A
Signs of hypervitaminosis A, vision, liver function with high/chronic dosing
summary: Vitamin A (retinol and its esters) is an essential fat-soluble vitamin supplemented to prevent and treat vitamin A deficiency, which causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, impaired immunity, and (in children) increased morbidity and mortality from infection. It is required for vision (rhodopsin), epithelial differentiation, growth, reproduction, and immune function. Doses range from physiologic replacement up to high therapeutic doses for established deficiency or specific public-health regimens. The major safety concerns are dose-related: high doses are teratogenic and must be avoided in pregnancy (do not exceed about 10,000 IU/day), and chronic excessive intake causes hypervitaminosis A with hepatotoxicity, raised intracranial pressure, bone and skin changes, and other toxicity. Vitamin A is best absorbed with a fat-containing meal; it accumulates in the liver, so excess is cumulative.
indications: Treatment of vitamin A deficiency (including night blindness and xerophthalmia)
Prevention of vitamin A deficiency in at-risk populations and as supplementation in malabsorptive states
Reduction of childhood morbidity and mortality from vitamin A deficiency in deficient populations (public-health high-dose regimens)
Supplementation in measles in vitamin-A-deficient children per WHO guidance

dosage.d: Up to 100,000-200,000 IU/day for ~3 days, then 50,000 IU/day, per WHO/clinical protocol
dosage.n: Follow established deficiency-treatment schedules; avoid in pregnancy

dosage.d: Men ~900 mcg RAE (3,000 IU); women ~700 mcg RAE (2,310 IU) daily
Infants <6 mo 50,000 IU; 6-11 mo 100,000 IU; >=12 mo 200,000 IU, repeated per schedule
Do NOT exceed ~10,000 IU/day (3,000 mcg RAE) from supplements
dosage.n: Higher doses are teratogenic; prefer beta-carotene where supplementation is required

admin: Take oral vitamin A with food, ideally a meal containing fat, to maximize absorption
Use the lowest dose adequate to correct deficiency; account for vitamin A from all sources (diet, fortified foods, multivitamins, fish-liver oils)
For high-dose deficiency or public-health regimens, follow the specific WHO/clinical schedule and confirm the patient is not pregnant
In malabsorption, water-miscible or parenteral formulations may be needed under supervision
Counsel women of childbearing potential about avoiding high-dose vitamin A and the teratogenic risk
moa: Vitamin A and its active retinoid metabolites have several essential physiologic roles. In the retina, 11-cis-retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin, the visual pigment required for low-light (night) vision; deficiency impairs dark adaptation and causes night blindness. Retinoic acid acts as a ligand for nuclear retinoic-acid and retinoid-X receptors, regulating gene transcription that controls cellular differentiation and the integrity of epithelial tissues (skin, cornea/conjunctiva, mucosae). Vitamin A is also required for normal immune function, growth, bone development, spermatogenesis, and embryonic development. Supplementation restores these functions when intake is deficient.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to vitamin A preparations or excipients
relative: Hepatic disease (risk of hepatotoxicity with excess)
Renal impairment / dialysis (vitamin A can accumulate)
Concurrent use of oral retinoids (additive hypervitaminosis A)
monitor: Signs and symptoms of hypervitaminosis A with high or chronic dosing
Liver function with high-dose or prolonged use
Pregnancy status in women of childbearing potential

preg: Vitamin A is essential in pregnancy at recommended intakes, but HIGH doses are teratogenic and can cause congenital malformations; supplemental intake should generally not exceed about 10,000 IU/day. Avoid high-dose vitamin A and vitamin-A-derived retinoids in pregnancy; where supplementation is needed, beta-carotene (provitamin A) is preferred as it is not associated with teratogenicity.
lact: Vitamin A is present in human milk and recommended intakes during lactation are safe and beneficial. Avoid high-dose maternal supplementation; excessive maternal intake increases milk vitamin A concentrations.
renal: Patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those on dialysis, can accumulate vitamin A and are at increased risk of hypervitaminosis A; avoid routine high-dose supplementation and monitor for toxicity.
hepatic: The liver stores vitamin A, and chronic excess is hepatotoxic, potentially causing hepatomegaly, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Avoid high doses in patients with liver disease, and use supplementation cautiously with monitoring of hepatic function.

major: Oral retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin, etretinate) and high-dose vitamin A - additive risk of hypervitaminosis A and teratogenicity; avoid combination
moderate: Orlistat and other fat-absorption inhibitors / bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) - reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamin A
Anticoagulants (warfarin) - large doses of vitamin A may augment anticoagulant effect/bleeding risk
Hepatotoxic drugs - additive hepatotoxicity with excess vitamin A
minor: Mineral oil reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin A
interactions.food: Take with a fat-containing meal to enhance absorption; account for dietary and fortified-food vitamin A.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid heavy alcohol use - alcohol and vitamin A excess are additively hepatotoxic.
interactions.diagnostics: Chronic excess may elevate serum vitamin A, liver enzymes, calcium, and lipids; can raise intracranial pressure (papilledema on exam).

common: With higher doses: nausea, headache, fatigue, dry skin/lips, irritability

Raised intracranial pressure / pseudotumor cerebri (headache, papilledema, vision changes)
Teratogenicity with high-dose use in pregnancy
rare: Bone pain, hypercalcemia, and bone changes with chronic excess
Bulging fontanelle in infants given high doses
emergency: Signs of raised intracranial pressure (severe headache, vomiting, vision changes, papilledema)

Signs of hypervitaminosis A with high-dose or prolonged therapy
Liver function tests with chronic/high-dose use
Serum vitamin A and calcium where toxicity is suspected
Pregnancy status before high-dose regimens in women of childbearing potential
counsel: Take vitamin A with a meal that contains some fat to help your body absorb it
Do not take more than prescribed - too much vitamin A builds up in the body and can be harmful, including to the liver
If you are pregnant or might become pregnant, do not take high-dose vitamin A, as it can cause birth defects
Tell your doctor about all supplements and multivitamins so your total vitamin A is not too high
Report severe headaches, blurred vision, vomiting, bone pain, peeling skin, or yellowing of the skin/eyes
Avoid heavy alcohol use while taking vitamin A supplements
pk: Deficiency signs (e.g., night blindness) improve over days to weeks
Serum retinyl esters peak ~4 hours after an oral dose
Stored in the liver; turnover is slow (weeks), reflecting large hepatic reserves
Hepatic stores sustain levels long after dosing - excess is cumulative
Store in a cool, dry place protected from light; keep capsules tightly closed
pearls: TERATOGENIC at high dose - do not exceed ~10,000 IU/day in pregnancy; prefer beta-carotene if supplementation is needed
Chronic excess causes hypervitaminosis A: hepatotoxicity, raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri), bone/skin changes - the liver stores it, so toxicity is cumulative
Take with a fat-containing meal for absorption; malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, orlistat) lowers levels
WHO high-dose regimens reduce child mortality in deficient populations and are given in measles for deficient children
Accumulates in chronic kidney disease and with concurrent oral retinoids - avoid high doses
Additive hepatotoxicity with alcohol and with oral retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin)
missed: If you miss a dose of a vitamin A supplement, take it when you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not take a double dose. Do not take extra to make up for missed doses, as excess vitamin A can be harmful.
overdose: Acute overdose (very large single dose) causes nausea, vomiting, headache, drowsiness, irritability, and in infants a bulging fontanelle and raised intracranial pressure; skin may peel days later. Chronic overdose (hypervitaminosis A) causes headache, raised intracranial pressure, dry/peeling skin, hair loss, bone and joint pain, hepatomegaly, and hyperlipidemia/hypercalcemia. There is no specific antidote: discontinue vitamin A and provide supportive care; most features resolve over days to weeks as stores fall. Treat raised intracranial pressure and other toxicity symptomatically.
